newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Austria opens crack in EMU interpretation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Austria opens crack in EMU interpretation.

text.p: Austria's National Bank on Thursday said the entry criteria for Europe's currency union were open to political interpretation, putting it on a potential collision course with its powerful German neighbour.
Central bank director Adolf Wala told reporters the strict thresholds laid down in the 1992 Maastricht treaty on European monetary union (EMU) were open to political interpretation.
"Within the treaty, there is political room for interpreting the three percent and the 60 percent criteria," he said. "They are not strictly three and not strictly 60 percent."
The treaty stipulates a range of economic targets for countries wanting to join EMU, including limiting budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and public debt to 60 percent.

Top German officials, eager to convince a sceptical public that the planned euro will be as hard as the mark, have over the past few weeks repeatedly reaffirmed their commitment to a strict adherence to the criteria.
The Bundesbank, traditionally the anchor of monetary stability in Europe, has also voiced strong objection to any watering down of the EMU critieria or a delay of the project.
"Wala sometimes has his own opinions," said a fixed income analyst at a leading Austrian bank, adding there was "certainly a discrepancy" between Wala's and the Bundesbank's views.
Many experts, as well as the European Union, forecast that Germany's deficit would exceed the target, fuelling speculation about a possible delay in the start of EMU.
German participation is seen as crucial to the success of the project, which is scheduled to start in 1999.
The European Commission on Wednesday forecast Germany would just squeeze in with a 1997 deficit forecast at three percent.

Austria itself is convinced it will be among the first members to qualify for early EMU membership, even though its debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to overshoot the 60 percent mark by anywhere up to nine percent.
"The debate about postponing monetary union is superfluous, if not damaging," Austrian central bank president Klaus Liebscher told a news conference earlier on Thursday.
"Austria is ready for EMU," he added.

Austria has long been one of Germany's closest monetary allies. Its currency, the schilling, has for the better part of the past two decades been closely tied to the mark and has hardly ever strayed from its central parity of seven schillings to the mark.
The link remained unchanged even after Austria joined the European Union and its exchange rate mechanism, seen as a precursor to EMU, in 1995.

Wala confirmed Austria did not consider any change in its policy of following Germany's monetary lead. "We will not change our monetary concept," he said, adding that the link with the mark had resulted in substantial benefits for the Austrian economy.
